lesson.grammar_point: modal verbs for certainty, possibility and obligation
phases: The Words of the Day After

listenings.text: I sit on four boards and I hear the same thing go wrong in almost every founder presentation. Somebody asks how fast something can happen, and the founder says we will do it in ninety days. He meant we are capable of ninety days. Those are not the same sentence. The one he said goes into the minutes as a commitment, and six months later, when it has taken a hundred and twenty for reasons that were never his, somebody reads it back to him in a room. And I want to be clear that this is not a non-native speaker problem. Native speakers do it constantly. You reach for the strongest word available because you want to sound confident, and the strongest word is almost never the accurate one. So here is what I tell people. Say what you are capable of. Then stop, and say separately what you will commit to. Make the two sentences audibly different, and let the room hear the difference. Nobody has ever thought less of a founder for that.

I have run around thirty integrations now, and almost none of the failures happen at the price. They happen in the ninety days after the money moves. The first thing that has to be decided is governance, and I mean it very literally: who decides what, and who has to be told. If that is not agreed before closing it will not get agreed after, because after closing everybody is busy and nobody wants the argument. The second thing is retention, and here I will tell you what I actually listen for. When a founder tells me all of my people will stay, I write nothing down, because nobody believes that and it tells me nothing. When a founder says three of my eleven might leave and here is which three, that is the person I trust with the rest of the plan. Honesty about the risk is not a weakness in that meeting. It is the only evidence I have that the rest of what you said is real.
